Watched in the built-in browser 2026-11-19: frames 0-66 s every 0.5-4 s (count-up burst 8-13 s), then 78/100/125/152/175/198/232/252/296 s and a played stretch 584-640 s (frame every ~4 s); word timings from YouTube's transcript panel (2,380 words, about 146 a minute incl. pauses); sound probe 584-639 s. Our own descriptions; shots after 66 s are spot samples, not a full list.

lines.gist: A dated auction: a giant plush monster sells for a car-sized price.
Its maker briefly outvalued the three biggest Western toy firms combined.
Six months on, resale prices and the share price have collapsed.
No rival did it; one textbook decision by the company did.
Channel pitch and subscribe ask, placed right after the promise.
Origin of the character with an illustrator, then a licence deal.
The retailer's founder and how blind boxes became the business model.
A pop star's post lights the fuse; sales spike, then keep growing.
Three layers of the machine: gamble, scarcity, resale value.
Scarcity turns ugly: fights, thefts, counterfeits.
The textbook fix, make more, removes the very thing people paid for.
Resale prices crash while reported revenue still soars.
Record results, falling stock, then slowing sales and swelling inventory.
The comeback plan: new characters, a film, Europe, buybacks.
Asks viewers for their stories, gives three labelled lessons, subscribe and disclaimer.

whyItWorks: Opens on a dated, concrete scene with a shocking price, then a bigger comparison, then the fall, then the promise of one decision, all inside 61 s.
Every figure is a designed object: a count-up over footage, a resale-app card whose price flips, a split-flap ticker, a ghost-free bar race with logos.
One consistent design system (charcoal or paper card, mint accent, italic serif asides, label-maker tapes) makes cheap stock and news clips look authored.
A curiosity title paired with a toy everyone has seen; the video answers a question the viewer already has.
